Then, finally, exam day arrived. Xiaoran honestly thought she might faint.

“This is the end,” she whispered outside the classroom.

Yichen straightened the crooked ribbon in her hair.

“You studied enough.”

“What if the test hates me personally?”

“It doesn’t know you.”

“That’s exactly why.”

Yichen laughed and squeezed her hand once.

“Just breathe first. Panic later.”

“Okay.”

Then, after a pause—

“…What if I fail?”

“You won’t.”

“How do you know?”

“Because,” he said, “I trust you.”

That sentence followed Xiaoran into the exam room and stayed there, quietly calming her every time the panic started to rise. One question at a time. For once, her brain didn’t completely betray her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later, results were posted. The hallway exploded with noise. Students crowded around the score sheets while teachers tried to keep order. Yuhao scanned the math rankings. Then he froze.

“…No way.”

Meilin looked over. “What?”

Yuhao pointed at the top of the list. One hundred. Lin Xiaoran. Silence. Then—

“AAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHH—”

The hallway practically shook. Xiaoran screamed loud enough to alert the neighboring buildings.

“I DID IT—”

She nearly tackled Meilin.

“MEILIN I’M ACADEMICALLY VALIDATED.”

“You’re crushing my lungs.”

Yichen pushed through the crowd toward the screaming. The second Xiaoran saw him, she ran straight into him.

“YICHEN.”

He caught her automatically and blinked down at her.

“…Why are you vibrating?”

“I GOT ONE HUNDRED.”

Silence. Real surprise crossed his face.

“…You did?”

“I DID.”

For a full second, Yichen just stared at her. Then he laughed—bright and proud, like he couldn’t help it. That look on his face felt even better than the score.

“I’m literally a genius now,” Xiaoran announced, clinging to him.

“You got one hundred once.”

“EXACTLY.”

Yichen smiled and brushed her hair away from her face.

“I told you you could do it.”

“I thought you were lying romantically.”

“I was academically sincere.”

Xiaoran looked up at him.

“…You’re really proud of me huh?”

Yichen paused. Then, more softly—

“Very.”

Oh. Oh no. That voice again—soft and proud, the one that did strange things to her heart. Xiaoran buried her face in his chest.

“This is so embarrassing.”

“You’re the one screaming.”

“I EARNED IT.”

Nearby, Yuhao looked traumatized.

“She beat half the basketball team.”

Meilin sighed. “Love is terrifying.”

Yichen held on to Xiaoran while she celebrated like she’d won the Olympics. Watching her smile like that, over something she had worked so hard for, might have been one of his favorite victories too.

chapters.desc: Months of dating, one nosy question at lunch, and a first kiss that goes almost perfectly.
chapters.title: The First Kiss Was Absolutely Not Smooth
chapters.epigraph: “The best first kisses are never the smooth ones.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had always assumed her first kiss would feel like a movie. Soft wind. Perfect timing. Music playing somewhere. Her actual first kiss with Zhou Yichen involved panic, overthinking, and nearly falling off a chair. Which honestly suited them better.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started because Tang Meilin asked one dangerous question at lunch.

“You two still haven’t kissed?”

Silence. Across the cafeteria table, Xiaoran choked on her drink. Zhou Yichen kept eating, perfectly calm. Yuhao looked horrified.

“WAIT.”

He pointed back and forth between them.

“You’re telling me you’ve been dating for months and still no kiss?!”

Xiaoran went red.

“WHY ARE YOU YELLING.”

“That’s insane.”

“It’s not insane!”

“It’s a medical phenomenon.”

Yichen went on eating his noodles like his girlfriend wasn’t combusting beside him. Traitor. Meilin looked genuinely curious.

“But seriously,” she asked, “why not?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it. She didn’t actually know. It just… had never happened. They held hands all the time. They hugged. Yichen kissed her forehead constantly. But an actual kiss? Every time the mood got even slightly romantic, Xiaoran panicked and ruined it. Once, she sneezed directly into his shoulder. Another time, she headbutted him trying to lean in. A tragedy. Yuhao looked at Yichen accusingly.

“How are YOU this patient?”

Yichen finally glanced up.

“She gets nervous.”

Xiaoran looked offended.

“You exposed me publicly.”

“You expose yourself naturally.”

“Wow.”

But afterward, something dangerous happened: Xiaoran couldn’t stop thinking about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few days were unbearable. Not because Yichen had changed. That was the problem. He was completely normal. He still held her hand, still smiled at her, still fixed her hair without thinking while he talked. Xiaoran, on the other hand, was in crisis. Suddenly every tiny interaction felt suspiciously romantic.

Like now: Friday evening, an empty classroom, sunset spilling through the windows while Yichen sorted the class notes. Outside, the basketball team was still yelling on the court. And Xiaoran was not okay. Why did his hands look nice arranging papers? Why did his voice sound warmer in empty rooms? Why was she suddenly aware of his lips existing?! This was horrible.

“You’re staring again,” Yichen said, without looking up.

Xiaoran nearly died.

“I’m not.”

“Hm.”

“I’m observing academically.”

“You once called fractions arrogant.”

“That’s unrelated.”

Yichen finally looked at her properly, and paused. She looked nervous. Actually nervous. It was very cute.

“What’s wrong?” he asked, more gently.

“…Nothing.”

“Liar.”

Xiaoran looked away. How was she supposed to explain this? Hello, boyfriend, your face has been causing me problems lately. Impossible. Yichen studied her for another moment. Then he understood. The corner of his mouth tipped up. Xiaoran noticed.

“…Why are you smiling like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you know secrets.”

“Maybe I do.”

Panic. Immediate panic. Xiaoran shot to her feet.

“I suddenly remembered responsibilities.”

She tried to escape. Zhou Yichen caught her wrist before she could get away. Not hard. Just enough to stop her.

“Running away?” he asked softly.

“No.”

“You stood up.”

“I’m exercising.”

Yichen laughed quietly. In the empty, sunset-lit classroom, the sound felt dangerously intimate. Xiaoran’s heartbeat was becoming a medical concern. Then Yichen drew her closer—slowly, giving her every chance to step away. She didn’t. Which was somehow scarier.

“You know,” he murmured, “you’ve been acting weird all week.”

Xiaoran looked everywhere except his eyes.

“I wonder why.”

“I think I know.”

“…Don’t say it out loud.”

“Why not?”

“Because I’ll die.”

Yichen smiled helplessly. Then, more quietly—

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Look at me.”

Slowly, she did. Big mistake. Zhou Yichen looking at her that gently should be illegal. Especially this close—close enough to count his eyelashes, close enough to feel how warm he was, close enough that breathing had become difficult. And somehow he looked calmer than ever, while Xiaoran was one second from cardiac arrest.

“You’re nervous,” he whispered.

“No I’m not.”

“You’re shaking.”

“That’s natural body activity.”

He laughed softly again, then lifted a hand and brushed her hair behind her ear. The movement was unbearably gentle. Suddenly the room felt quieter. Real. Her heartbeat was so loud she wondered if he could hear it.

“Yichen,” she whispered.

“Hm?”

“If you keep looking at me like that, I’m going to explode.”

“That sounds inconvenient.”

“It IS.”

He smiled a little. Then his face softened completely—warm, patient, like he was waiting for her instead of rushing her. He was always waiting for her. That alone nearly melted her. Then, very softly, Yichen asked:

“Can I kiss you?”

Somehow, the fact that he asked made everything so much worse. Xiaoran stared at him for two seconds, then nodded way too fast. Instantly embarrassing.

“Oh my god,” she whispered. “That looked desperate.”

Yichen laughed quietly—and then he leaned in and kissed her. It was soft and warm and gentle enough that Xiaoran’s brain stopped working entirely. For one beautiful second, everything was still. No music. No fireworks. Just Zhou Yichen holding her like she was something precious. Then Xiaoran lost her balance and nearly toppled backward off her chair. Yichen caught her, laughing into her shoulder. Mortifying. Absolutely mortifying.

“I hate this,” Xiaoran mumbled into his chest.

“You hate kissing me?”

“No. I hate having bones and embarrassment.”

Yichen smiled helplessly and set her upright again. Her face was still bright red. He, unfairly, looked calm—except for the tips of his ears, which had gone pink.

“How are YOU normal right now?” she accused.

“I’m not normal.”

“You look normal.”

“That’s because someone almost fell to her death after one kiss.”

“That sounds dramatic when you say it like that.”

“It was dramatic.”

Xiaoran buried her face in his shoulder.

“This relationship humiliates me constantly.”

Yichen laughed and kissed the top of her head this time—gentler, familiar. Somehow that tiny second kiss felt even more dangerous. Because now Lin Xiaoran finally understood what all the fuss was about. A tragic realization, honestly.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran wanted one proper date. She didn’t expect a street band to describe her relationship out loud.
chapters.title: The Song That Knew Too Much
chapters.epigraph: “Some songs sound like they were written about you. Some actually were.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s dates usually ended in chaos, not romance. Most weekends meant Chen Yuhao screaming at video games in somebody’s living room while Tang Meilin judged everyone from the couch. Yichen would sit beside Xiaoran. Xiaoran would steal his hoodie. And the whole afternoon would disappear without either of them noticing. So when Xiaoran announced—

“We’re going on a REAL date tomorrow.”

—everyone reacted differently. Yuhao nearly choked. Meilin looked suspicious. Zhou Yichen just looked amused.

On Saturday morning, sunlight filled Xiaoran’s bedroom while she tore through her wardrobe. Today mattered. Not that she would admit it. Okay, maybe a little. The problem was Douyin. All week, her feed had been full of ridiculously aesthetic couples walking down pretty streets, holding hands, soft music playing. Now Xiaoran wanted that too. Just once. A proper date. Just the two of them. No basketball, no friends, no Yuhao screaming “GET A ROOM” every ten minutes. And sometimes she missed him, even though she saw him almost every day. Which sounded insane. But it was true.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You look nervous,” Yichen said the second Xiaoran climbed into the car he’d borrowed from his dad.

“I’m not nervous.”

“You changed outfits three times.”

“How do YOU know that?”

“You posted mirror selfies accidentally.”

“…Oh.”

Yichen laughed and handed her a milk tea. Half sugar, no pearls. Of course he remembered. Xiaoran’s carefully prepared cool image cracked a little.

“You’re trying to emotionally manipulate me already,” she accused.

“It’s 10 a.m.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen smiled at the road. Zhou Yichen out of his school uniform was a problem. Grey sweater. A watch loose around his wrist. Hair a little messy from the wind. It was upsetting. Xiaoran stared too long. Yichen noticed.

“You’re doing it again.”

“What?”

“Staring.”

“I’m observing.”

“That sounds scientific.”

“It is.”

“What’s your conclusion?”

Xiaoran turned to the window.

“…My boyfriend looks like a perfume ad.”

Yichen nearly laughed into the steering wheel.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date went surprisingly well. They wandered through shopping streets, shared snacks, and argued over claw machines. Xiaoran lost six tries at a plush rabbit before Yichen won it on his first—exactly like the day they met.

“Show-off,” she muttered, hugging it anyway.

“You spent twenty yuan.”

“It was a strategic investment.”

At one point they stopped at a tiny café Xiaoran had found on Douyin. The desserts were beautiful. The portions were microscopic.

“People online lied to me,” Xiaoran whispered while staring at her tiny cake.

“You wanted aesthetics.”

“I also wanted survival.”

Yichen pushed half of his toward her without a word. Zhou Yichen always remembered things. He noticed things, and quietly took care of her before she even asked: picking the cilantro out of her noodles, catching her wrist when she drifted toward the road, carrying her bag after she complained exactly once. Those tiny things softened her heart more than any grand gesture could.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening, the streets had gone quiet. Golden light stretched across the sidewalks, and the little shops switched on their warm lights one by one. Xiaoran walked beside Yichen, swinging their joined hands.

“Tired?” he asked.

“No.”

“You walked slower.”

“I’m preserving the date.”

Yichen looked amused. “That’s not how time works.”

“You don’t know romance.”

Then music drifted down the street. A small student band was playing outside a café on the riverside corner. Nothing fancy—a guitarist, a keyboard player, and a singer laughing shyly at the little crowd that had gathered. Xiaoran stopped walking.

“Ooooh.”

She tugged Yichen to the back of the crowd. The singer adjusted the microphone and smiled.

“This next song is dedicated,” he said lightly, “to people who accidentally fell in love with someone troublesome.”

The crowd laughed softly. Beside Yichen, Xiaoran gasped.

“Wow,” she whispered. “That’s targeted harassment against you.”

Yichen glanced down.

“Interesting. I thought it sounded like you.”

“Rude.”

Then the guitar started, soft and warm, the kind of melody that belonged to sunsets. The singer began—

“She talks too much when she gets excited,
Gets angry over things that don’t matter,
Cries when I tease her even a little—
But somehow the world gets quieter beside her.”

Xiaoran blinked once.

“…Wait.”

Yichen’s lips twitched. The singer continued.

“She steals my jackets like they belong to her,
Complains every day but still waits for me after class,
Everyone says she’s hard to handle—
So why do I keep smiling when I see her?”

That line was a little too accurate. Yichen laughed under his breath. Xiaoran turned slowly.

“…Why are you laughing.”

Yichen looked away, still smiling.

“This song is suspicious.”

“What does that mean?”

“It knows too much.”

Xiaoran squinted at him as the music softened into the chorus.

“Maybe love isn’t peaceful after all,
Maybe love is noisy and clingy and impossible,
But if she disappeared for even one day—
I think my whole life would feel empty.”

Silence. A breeze moved down the street. Cars passed. Somewhere behind them, people were laughing. But Zhou Yichen couldn’t really hear any of it anymore. Every lyric kept turning into Lin Xiaoran: her dramatic voice, the way she’d clung to him before his family trip, her tiny angry face when she was jealous, the way she filled every silence without trying, the way even the worst days got lighter once she showed up. And the chorus was painfully true. If Xiaoran disappeared from his life now, everything really would feel emptier.

Beside him, Xiaoran had stopped joking too. When she looked up, Yichen was already looking at her—quietly, softly, like the song had just told everyone his secrets.

“…Stop looking at me like that,” she muttered.

“Like what?”

“Like YOU wrote the lyrics.”

Yichen smiled a little, then leaned in just enough that only she could hear—

“The chorus is true though.”

Xiaoran’s face went red.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You can’t suddenly say romantic things during public music events.”

“That sounds oddly specific.”

“I’m serious.”

Yichen laughed and laced his fingers through hers a little tighter. The singer moved into the last verse—

“She’ll probably never realize this,
But every ordinary day became brighter after meeting her,
So if loving her means losing my peace forever—
Then honestly… I don’t mind at all.”

And for the first time that whole day, Lin Xiaoran understood why people loved romance songs so much. Not because the lyrics were dramatic. Because when you were standing next to the right person, every line sounded true.

chapters.desc: Her cousin and her boyfriend are spending Saturday together. Lin Xiaoran has concerns.
chapters.title: Lin Jun Stole Her Boyfriend for a Day
chapters.epigraph: “The scariest meeting isn’t meeting the parents. It’s meeting the cousin who knows everything.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen smiled at his phone during lunch. Not a normal smile. A suspicious one. She narrowed her eyes.

“Who are you texting.”

Yichen glanced up. “Lin Jun.”

“My cousin?” Xiaoran repeated slowly.

“Hm.”

“…Why.”

“He asked if I wanted to hang out Saturday.”

A longer silence. Then Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Absolutely not.”

Across the table, Chen Yuhao looked delighted. “Oho.”

Tang Meilin didn’t even look up from her phone. Everyone had seen this coming. Ever since Lin Jun moved back from Shanghai for a new job, he and Zhou Yichen had gotten along disgustingly well. It made no sense. One was Xiaoran’s emotionally exhausted older cousin. The other was her emotionally exhausted boyfriend. Apparently shared suffering created male friendship. Traitors. Both of them.

“Why are YOU two hanging out?” Xiaoran demanded.

Yichen looked unbothered. “He wants to know me better.”

“That sounds like an interrogation.”

Yuhao nodded seriously. “It probably is.”

Meilin sipped her drink calmly. “Honestly fair.”

“WHOSE SIDE ARE YOU ON?”

Nobody answered, because Lin Jun investigating Zhou Yichen was extremely understandable. If Xiaoran dated some random guy, her family would absolutely run a background check. Still, Xiaoran hated it. Somehow, she felt left out. Which was ridiculous. But true.

“You’re stealing my boyfriend,” she told Jun on a video call that evening.

Lin Jun looked completely relaxed.

“He’ll survive.”

“That’s not the issue.”

“What is the issue?”

“You two are bonding without supervision.”

Jun laughed.

“Why do you sound like a worried mother?”

“Because you’re suspicious.”

From the corner of the screen, Yichen sipped his water and watched the argument unfold, thoroughly entertained. Traitor.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came, and Lin Xiaoran became the most restless person alive.

“This feels wrong,” she muttered, pacing Meilin’s bedroom.

Meilin, lying on her bed with a face mask on, already looked exhausted.

“It’s one afternoon.”

“My cousin and boyfriend are going on a date.”

“It’s not a date.”

“How do YOU know.”

“Because one of them basically raised you.”

“That doesn’t stop men from being weird.”

Across the city, Zhou Yichen was finding the whole thing interesting. He liked Lin Jun. Calm, sharp, easy to talk to. And dangerously observant. The two of them were walking through a riverside shopping district with iced coffees.

“You know,” Jun said eventually, “Xiaoran thinks I’m stealing you.”

Yichen laughed.

“She told me that too.”

“And?”

“She sounded serious.”

“She probably is.”

Yichen smiled. Very Xiaoran. For a while, the conversation stayed easy—basketball, university, Jun’s years working in Shanghai. Then, naturally, it turned to Xiaoran.

“How long have you liked her?” Jun asked.

Yichen thought about it.

“…Longer than she realized.”

Jun nodded, like that made sense. After a moment—

“She’s difficult sometimes.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s true.”

“But.” Jun glanced sideways briefly. “She’s sincere.”

“I know.”

“She gets attached deeply to people.”

Yichen knew that too, probably better than anyone now. Lin Xiaoran loved loudly, clingily, like she had never learned how to hold back. Maybe that was why he liked her so much.

“She talks about you constantly,” Jun added.

Yichen sighed. “Apparently everyone knows that.”

“Trust me. You have no idea.”

Jun stopped outside a small convenience store.

“You know what she used to do as a kid?”

Yichen sensed danger.

“What?”

“She cried because I went on a school trip for three days.”

“Oh my god,” said Xiaoran’s voice behind them.

Both men turned. There she was, three meters away with Meilin, looking deeply betrayed.

Jun blinked. “What are you doing here?”

“You shared your location accidentally.”

Then Yichen laughed so hard he nearly dropped his drink. Jun looked horrified.

“You TRACKED me?”

“I had emotional concerns.”

“You’re insane.”

“You STOLE MY BOYFRIEND.”

A woman walking her dog gave them a wide berth. Meilin covered her face.

“I told her not to come.”

“You participated willingly,” Xiaoran accused.

“I was kidnapped.”

Jun sighed and looked at Yichen.

“…You see what we dealt with growing up?”

Yichen smiled.

“Every day.”

Xiaoran marched over and grabbed Yichen’s sleeve.

“Are you done bonding?”

Jun looked offended.

“He likes me more than you now.”

“That’s fake.”

“You sure?”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Choose carefully.”

The threat would have been scarier if she weren’t holding his sleeve like an angry kitten. Yichen looked from one cousin to the other. Then he answered—

“He buys me coffee.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Jun nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran looked devastated.

“Wow,” she whispered. “Betrayed by family and romance at the same time.”

Yichen finally smiled and pulled her closer by the wrist. Then, near her ear—

“You know no one replaces you.”

Instant recovery. Meilin watched in disgust.

“Disgusting.”

Jun nodded solemnly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran had already cheered up. Maybe Lin Jun and Zhou Yichen getting along wasn’t the worst thing. Especially since they both already looked equally exhausted from dealing with her. A true family connection, really.

chapters.desc: One bad landing in a close game, and Lin Xiaoran learns what real fear feels like.
chapters.title: Don’t Scare Me Like That Again
chapters.epigraph: “Some people love quietly. She loved like a fire alarm.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated basketball injuries. Not normal hate. Personal hate. Basketball injuries meant blood, limping, bruises, and Zhou Yichen saying “I’m fine” while very obviously not fine. And Zhou Yichen got hurt often enough that Xiaoran had developed a small trauma response to the word “injury.” Usually it wasn’t serious. A sprained wrist. A bruised shoulder. A sore ankle. Things athletes shrugged off, and things Xiaoran absolutely did not. Still, even she knew basketball was rough. So normally, she saved the drama for afterward.

Today was different.

✦ ✦ ✦

Final quarter of the city league semifinal, and the gym was deafening. The score was close. Everyone was screaming. Xiaoran sat beside Meilin in the bleachers, clutching Yichen’s jacket in both hands.

“He looks tired,” she muttered, for the tenth time.

“He’s played three quarters nonstop,” Meilin said.

“But he looks EXTRA tired.”

“He’s sweating because he’s a human being.”

Xiaoran ignored her. Something felt wrong today. The game had turned rough early. One player on the other team kept going after Yichen—nothing technically illegal, just too physical. And Yichen, competitive Yichen, only got colder each quarter. More intense. More reckless.

Eventually, Meilin noticed too.

“…He’s getting irritated.”

On the court, Yichen blocked a shot and drove forward again, fast and sharp. The crowd roared. Then it all happened too fast. One shove. One bad landing. The horrible screech of sneakers skidding across the floor—and Zhou Yichen went down. Hard. The gym went silent. Xiaoran froze—her whole brain froze—because Yichen wasn’t getting up. He stayed down, gripping his leg, while players crowded around him. Coach Wang ran onto the court. A whistle. Someone in the crowd gasped.

And somewhere nearby, someone whispered—

“That looked bad.”

That sentence alone broke something in Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

Her voice came out small. Then louder—

“YICHEN.”

Meilin grabbed her wrist before she could run onto the court.

“Xiaoran wait—”

But Xiaoran couldn’t breathe properly. Yichen still wasn’t standing. Worse, he looked like he was in real pain—the kind he usually hid in a second. His face was pale, his jaw tight, his breathing uneven.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen had been helped to the bench, Xiaoran was crying. Not dramatic crying. Real tears. The medical staff examined his ankle while Coach Wang argued with the referees.

“It’s probably a bad sprain,” Meilin said gently.

Probably. Xiaoran hated that word. Probably still meant maybe not. Finally, Yichen looked up—straight at the bleachers, straight at her. The second he saw her crying, the pain on his face gave way to something else: worry. For her. Even now. Idiot. He mouthed something: I’m okay. Xiaoran nearly cried harder, because he was so obviously NOT okay.

✦ ✦ ✦

The game ended eventually. Xiaoran didn’t remember the score, or the crowd leaving, or anyone talking to her. She only remembered rushing to the medical room afterward with shaking hands and pushing the door open. Yichen was sitting on the examination bed while the doctor wrapped his ankle. He looked up when she came in.

“…Hey.”

That one word nearly undid her.

“You scared me,” she whispered.

Yichen paused. Then his expression softened. He could tell she’d been genuinely terrified. Xiaoran walked closer, trying very hard not to cry again. She failed.

“Does it hurt badly?”

“A little.”

“That means yes.”

“A reasonable amount.”

“What does THAT mean?!”

Yichen managed a weak smile, which somehow made it worse. Why was he comforting her? He was the one who was hurt. The doctor finished and stood.

“No fractures,” he explained calmly. “But severe sprain. He needs proper rest.”

Rest. Thank god. Not surgery, not the hospital, not permanent damage. The second the doctor left, Xiaoran let out a shaky breath, maybe her first in an hour. Then she hit Yichen’s shoulder. Not hard.

“I hate you.”

Yichen blinked.

“That seems harsh.”

“You fell like you were dying.”

“I twisted my ankle.”

“You scared me to death.”

Her voice cracked on the last word, and Yichen’s face went soft. This wasn’t Xiaoran being dramatic. She had genuinely panicked—probably imagined the worst possible ending in the first three seconds.

“…Come here,” he said quietly.

Xiaoran was beside him before he finished saying it. Yichen pulled her carefully against him, one hand at the back of her head. Only then did Xiaoran notice how cold her hands had gone.

“I’m okay,” he murmured into her hair.

“You weren’t moving.”

“I know.”

“You looked hurt.”

“I was hurt.”

“That’s worse.”

Yichen laughed under his breath—then hissed when he moved wrong. Xiaoran pulled back.

“SEE.”

“Relax.”

“DON’T RELAX.”

He smiled helplessly. This was exactly why he hid injuries from her sometimes. Lin Xiaoran loved catastrophically. The second something happened to someone she cared about, her feelings went straight to maximum. Sometimes he found that kind of love a little overwhelming. But never unwanted. Never that.

“You know,” he said after a while, “players get injured all the time.”

“I know.”

“Then why were you crying like someone announced my funeral?”

“Because it was YOU.”

She said it without even thinking, and it hit harder than he expected. Yichen looked at her for a second—her red eyes, the worry she still couldn’t hide—then gently brushed his thumb under her eye.

“You really got scared huh?”

Xiaoran tried to glare.

“You think?”

“I’m sorry.”

Zhou Yichen rarely apologized for getting hurt. It usually wasn’t his fault. But he meant this one, like he regretted scaring her more than the injury itself. Xiaoran sniffed.

“You better recover properly.”

“Hm.”

“And no pretending you’re okay just to practice again.”

“Hm.”

“And no acting cool.”

“That one’s difficult.”

She hit his shoulder again. Yichen laughed and caught her hand this time, lacing their fingers together. Comforting her again, without even thinking about it. Outside the medical room, the evening light was fading across the empty gym. The match was long over. The crowd was gone. Everything had finally gone quiet. Only then did Xiaoran realize something embarrassing: her heartbeat had only calmed down once she was holding Zhou Yichen’s hand again.

chapters.desc: Three weeks off the court. One girlfriend in full nurse mode. Zhou Yichen may not survive his own recovery.
chapters.title: Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.
chapters.epigraph: “The injury healed in weeks. The worry took longer.”
chapters.content:
The aftermath of Zhou Yichen’s injury was unbearable for exactly one reason: Lin Xiaoran, treating him like a critically endangered patient.

“Walk slower.”

“I am walking.”

“You limped emotionally.”

“That’s not medically possible.”

“It looked painful.”

Yichen was standing by his locker while Xiaoran hovered nearby like an anxious ghost. It had been three days since the injury, and somehow she had gotten worse instead of calmer. The sprain meant no basketball for at least three weeks, which annoyed Yichen enough already. Xiaoran was acting like he’d come back from a war. Yesterday she’d carried his bag, even though it was clearly too heavy for her. This morning she’d bought him breakfast, water, AND vitamins. At lunch she’d pulled out his chair for him.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“I injured my ankle.”

“Yes.”

“Not my entire body.”

“You don’t know how interconnected health is.”

Across the classroom, Yuhao looked deeply entertained.

“She’s entered nurse mode.”

Meilin nodded solemnly. “Dangerous stage.”

“I can hear both of you,” Xiaoran snapped.

Two seconds later—

“Yichen don’t stand too long.”

Yichen sighed into his hand. The worst part was that he couldn’t stop her. Every time he said he was fine, her eyes went watery. It was psychological warfare.

✦ ✦ ✦

Things got worse after school, because Zhou Yichen made one terrible mistake: he forgot Xiaoran was behind him on the stairs and walked a little faster than usual.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The entire hallway turned. Yichen stopped. Behind him, Xiaoran looked genuinely horrified.

“Why are you moving like that?!”

“…Like a human?”

“You’re injured.”

“My legs still function.”

“Not correctly.”

Before he could argue, Xiaoran took his arm. Not dramatically, this time. Carefully, like she was afraid too much pressure might hurt him. Yichen felt guilty instead of amused. She still looked shaken from that day.

“You know,” he said more softly as they went down the stairs, “I’m recovering fine.”

“I know.”

“But?”

Xiaoran looked away. Then, quieter—

“When you fell…” She swallowed slightly. “You really scared me.”

Oh. There it was again—the fear she couldn’t hide. Yichen remembered it too: the crying, her shaking hands, the way she’d looked at him like the world had almost ended. Part of him still felt bad for putting that look on her face.

“You know I’d tell you if it was serious right?” he murmured.

Xiaoran nodded. Then, after a pause—

“But you also always say you’re fine even when you’re not.”

That was fair. Yichen sighed.

“I hate when you’re reasonable.”

“I learned from Meilin.”

“Dangerous friendship.”

Finally, Xiaoran smiled a little, small and relieved, and somehow that smile made Yichen less annoyed about the whole injury.

✦ ✦ ✦

The peace lasted about twelve hours. The next morning, Xiaoran was back in full disaster mode.

“Why are you carrying THAT.”

Yichen blinked. He was holding a bag of basketballs outside the gym storeroom.

“…Because Coach asked?”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

Yichen stared at her. Xiaoran stared back. Then she marched over and took the bag right out of his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“You need rest.”

“It weighs five kilograms.”

“Exactly.”

“That’s not heavy.”

“To ME it is.”

“Then why are YOU carrying it?”

Silence. Xiaoran made it two steps before she started struggling. Nearby, Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing.

“This relationship is incredible.”

Meilin looked exhausted. “One of them has no survival instincts. The other has no logic.”

“WHICH ONE.”

“Both.”

Yichen took the bag back before Xiaoran hurt herself instead. Then, without thinking, he crouched and retied the shoelace she’d been stepping on all morning. It happened so casually that neither of them noticed. Yuhao did. Yuhao never missed a chance to be annoying.

“Oh my god,” he whispered. “You two are disgusting.”

Xiaoran went red.

“We literally did nothing.”

“He bent down like a husband in a drama.”

“SHUT UP.”

Yichen just smiled, stood up, and tapped her forehead.

“You’re worrying too much.”

“I’m not.”

“You almost cried because I carried basketballs.”

“That was a reasonable reaction.”

It was exhausting. It was also very cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, it started pouring after class. Most students waited by the entrance for parents or buses. Xiaoran sat beside Yichen and watched the rain hammer the courtyard. For once, she wasn’t talking. No complaining. Just quiet.

“Does it still hurt?”

Yichen glanced at his wrapped ankle.

“A little.”

“See.”

“It’s healing.”

“But still hurting.”

Yichen smiled helplessly. After a moment—

“Come here.”

Xiaoran shifted closer, and Yichen rested his chin on top of her head, holding her hand loosely.

“I’m okay,” he murmured again.

This time, Xiaoran didn’t argue. She leaned into him and whispered—

“…You can’t get seriously hurt.”

“Hm?”

“I don’t like it.”

It sounded so simple. Almost childish. But Yichen knew what she meant. She couldn’t stand seeing him in pain, or not knowing, or the idea of something bad happening to him. That kind of love scared him sometimes. Nobody had ever worried about him that fiercely before. Not even himself. Then Xiaoran added bitterly—

“You fell for three seconds and I already imagined widowhood.”

Yichen choked on a laugh.

“WIDOWHOOD?”

“I panicked.”

“We’re in high school.”

“That doesn’t stop tragedy.”

Yichen laughed so hard his ankle shifted wrong again.

“DON’T MOVE.”

“Okay okay.”

“See? SEE?”

He was still smiling while she scolded him. And for the first time since the injury, the fear they had both been carrying quietly started to fade.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran overhears that she’s holding Zhou Yichen back—and starts to wonder if they’re right.
chapters.title: Should We Break Up?
chapters.epigraph: “The cruelest words are the ones we quietly agree with.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran usually ignored rumors. Not because she was emotionally strong. She just didn’t care enough. People talked all the time anyway—about grades, relationships, appearances. Half the school practically ran on gossip. So whenever Xiaoran overheard someone talking about her, she usually rolled her eyes and walked away. This time, they mentioned Zhou Yichen too. And that changed everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened on a Thursday after class. Xiaoran had stayed late helping Meilin decorate classroom boards for school festival week.

By the time she finished, the hallways were almost empty. She was heading for the back staircase, texting Yichen, when she heard it.

“…Honestly, Zhou Yichen could do way better.”

Xiaoran slowed down. Girls’ voices, somewhere around the corner by the storage room. Normally she would have kept walking. Then—

“I don’t even understand what he sees in Lin Xiaoran.”

Silence. Xiaoran stopped. She didn’t mean to. Her feet just stopped. The voices went on.

“I heard he rejected training invitations because she wanted attention.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“No seriously. My friend from Class 3 said he skipped extra practice before because Xiaoran was upset.”

“She’s honestly holding him back.”

“And he used to be way more focused before dating.”

The girls laughed—not loudly, not cruelly. Just casually, like they really believed it. Somehow that was worse. Xiaoran stayed frozen, because the worst part was that some of it was technically true. A few weeks ago, Yichen really had turned down an extra match. But not because of her. She knew that. His ankle hadn’t fully healed, and Coach Wang had told him not to overdo it. Still, hearing people say she was dragging him down lodged painfully in her chest. Especially because… what if other people thought so too?

✦ ✦ ✦

After that day, something changed. Not dramatically. Quietly enough that only the people closest to Xiaoran noticed. She still smiled, still joked, still clung to Yichen. But sometimes she went quiet afterward, especially when basketball came up.

Like now: Saturday afternoon at Meilin’s house, everyone eating snacks while Yuhao rambled excitedly about an upcoming invitational tournament. Apparently several schools had asked for Yichen by name.

“Coach says scouts might come too,” Yuhao said proudly.

Meilin nodded. “That’s huge.”

Normally Xiaoran would have bragged like she’d personally trained Zhou Yichen herself. Today, she only smiled and looked down at her drink. Yichen noticed, of course.

Later that evening, walking her home, he finally asked—

“What’s wrong?”

Xiaoran blinked innocently.

“Hm?”

“You’ve been weird for two weeks.”

“I’m always weird.”

“Not like this.”

Silence. The evening wind moved softly through the quiet street. Then, more quietly—

“You stop talking whenever basketball gets mentioned.”

Oh. So he had noticed that too. Of course he had. Zhou Yichen noticed everything about her, even the moods she worked hardest to hide.

“…Nothing’s wrong,” she said eventually.

“Liar.”

He said it so simply, so certainly, that Xiaoran nearly cried right there. He knew her too well now. Yichen slowed down and looked at her properly.

“Did someone say something?”

The question landed too close. Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her sleeve, and Yichen understood. His expression cooled.

“Who?”

“No one.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked away. She didn’t want him angry. That wasn’t the point. The point was that the words wouldn’t leave her head. Holding him back. Distracting him. Making him less focused. She knew how talented Yichen was, how seriously everyone talked about his future. Meanwhile she still got lost near school and cried over math. The comparison suddenly felt unbearable.

“So what if they’re right?”

Yichen stopped walking.

“…What?”

Xiaoran stared straight ahead.

“I mean…” She forced a small laugh. “You were already doing so well before me.”

“Xiaoran.”

“And everyone expects so much from you.”

His expression changed. Serious now. Actually serious. But Xiaoran kept going before she could lose her nerve.

“What if dating me really makes things harder for you?”

Silence. Then, very quietly—

“Should we break up?”

The world went still. Even Xiaoran felt strange after saying it, like the sentence didn’t belong to her. Just thinking it already hurt. Zhou Yichen just looked at her. Not angry. Not shocked. Deeply focused, like he was trying to work out how she’d gotten there on her own.

“Who told you that?”

Xiaoran looked down.

“No one directly.”

“What exactly did they say?”

“…That I hold you back.”

Out loud, it sounded embarrassingly small. Yichen was quiet for two seconds. Then he laughed softly—not mocking, just disbelieving—and that confused Xiaoran even more.

“You’re laughing?”

“I’m trying very hard not to get angry.”

“Oh.”

Then he took her hand, lacing his fingers through hers.

“Look at me,” he said quietly.

Slowly, Xiaoran did, and immediately regretted it. He was looking at her far too softly.

“You think I’d choose basketball over you?”

“That’s not what I mea—”

“If dating you affected me negatively,” he continued calmly, “I would’ve ended things already.”

Xiaoran blinked. That was painfully logical.

“But instead,” he said more quietly, “you’re the person I want beside me after every game.”

“You’re the first person I look for in crowds.”

Another silence.

“And you think that makes my life worse?”

Xiaoran’s chest ached. Hearing him say it so directly was almost too much.

“But your future—”

“My future is my responsibility.”

He said it like he’d decided that a long time ago. Yichen sighed and stepped closer.

“You know why I skipped that extra match?”

Xiaoran nodded weakly. “Your ankle.”

“Exactly.” His thumb brushed lightly across her knuckles. “Not because of you.”

“I know.”

“Then why believe strangers over me?”

That question hurt the most, because she didn’t know. Maybe loving someone that talented made insecurity grow quietly. Like one day he might realize he deserved someone better. More mature. Less troublesome. Maybe Yichen understood that already, because he pulled her into his arms.

“You know what actually distracts me?” he murmured into her hair.

Xiaoran blinked.

“What?”

“You crying over imaginary breakups.”

“I hate you.”

“No you don’t.”

“That was manipulative.”

“It worked.”

Unfortunately, it had. Now Xiaoran just felt ridiculous—for overthinking alone this long, for almost believing strangers over Yichen. After a while, she muttered into his hoodie—

“…You really don’t want to break up?”

Yichen pulled back just enough to look at her properly. Then, flatly—

“Absolutely not.”

“Oh.”

“And honestly,” he added calmly, “you’re not escaping me that easily.”

Xiaoran laughed—her first real laugh in weeks.

“There she is,” Yichen murmured softly.

And just like that, Lin Xiaoran finally felt like herself again.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen eats chili oil like water. Lin Xiaoran decides to build a tolerance. It goes about as well as expected.
chapters.title: You’re Crying Over Chili Oil?
chapters.epigraph: “Love is wanting to share someone’s world, even when it burns.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had one frightening talent: he could eat spicy food like his tongue had signed a legal immunity contract. Not normal spicy. Unhinged spicy. The kind that made other people reconsider their life choices after one bite. And Zhou Yichen stayed calm, unbothered, completely fine. Lin Xiaoran absolutely hated it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s literally red.”

“That’s usually what chili oil looks like.”

“No,” Xiaoran whispered, staring at his noodles in horror. “That’s not food. That’s chemical warfare.”

The four of them were at a noodle shop near school after basketball practice. Rain was pouring outside. Yuhao was happily demolishing a plate of fried rice, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted as always, and Zhou Yichen was calmly adding MORE chili oil to an already dangerous bowl of noodles.

“You’re trying to impress someone.”

“I’m eating dinner.”

“That cannot taste good.”

Yichen glanced at her lazily. “Want to try?”

“Absolutely not.”

Three minutes later, Xiaoran stole a bite anyway, because curiosity always beat her survival instincts. Instant regret. Her soul nearly left her body.

“WATER.”

Yuhao choked laughing.

“She’s dying.”

“IT BURNS.”

“You took half the spoon.”

“I THOUGHT HE WAS EXAGGERATING.”

Yichen pushed his drink toward her before she could combust.

“Slow down.”

“YOU EAT THIS WILLINGLY?”

“It’s not that spicy.”

Meilin stared at him blankly. “You’ve lost human sensation.”

The noodle shop owner wandered over and set a glass of milk in front of Xiaoran without a word, like he’d seen this before. Accurate. Zhou Yichen kept eating peacefully while Xiaoran sat there blinking back tears from one bite. One. His bowl looked like lava.

“This relationship won’t survive long-term,” Xiaoran whispered afterward, clutching her iced tea.

“Because of chili oil?” Yichen asked.

“Yes.”

“That feels unreasonable.”

“No,” Yuhao interrupted seriously. “Actually dietary incompatibility destroys marriages.”

“Why are you talking like a divorced uncle?” Meilin asked tiredly.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, the spicy food situation got personal, because Zhou Yichen started teasing her about it. Subtly. Constantly. Very annoyingly. At lunch the next day—

“Want some?”

“No.”

“You sure?”

“Yes.”

“It’s mild.”

“You’re a liar.”

Yichen smiled a little and ate the noodles himself. No reaction. No suffering. No weakness. That annoyed Xiaoran most of all. How was he so handsome while casually eating lava? It felt biologically unfair.

One afternoon after school, Xiaoran finally snapped.

“I’m building spice tolerance.”

Yichen looked up from his homework.

“…Why.”

“So I can understand your world.”

“That sounds dramatic.”

“It IS dramatic.”

Meilin looked concerned.

“Please don’t.”

“Too late.”

Yuhao grinned. “This’ll be funny.”

It was not funny. Not even slightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first attempt was a disaster. Xiaoran bought “mild” skewers from a street stall after school. “Mild,” the vendor promised. Lies. Cruel lies.

Halfway through the second skewer, Xiaoran’s eyes were already streaming. Yichen sighed and handed her tissues.

“You don’t need to force yourself.”

“I can do this.”

“You’re crying.”

“That’s temporary weakness.”

She took another bite out of pure stubbornness and immediately coughed herself into another dimension. Yuhao had to lean against a wall to laugh.

“She looks betrayed by society.”

Meilin rubbed her forehead. “I knew this would happen.”

Yichen watched her—the stubborn face, the watery eyes, the way she kept going anyway. Hopelessly cute.

“Okay, enough,” he said, taking the skewer from her.

“No.”

“You stopped breathing earlier.”

“I’m adapting.”

“You’re dying.”

Xiaoran glared at him over her carton of milk. Then, after a moment—

“…How are you eating this normally?”

Yichen shrugged. “I grew up with it.”

“That sounds traumatic.”

“It’s food.”

“It’s violence.”

He laughed under his breath, then wiped a bit of sauce from the corner of her mouth with his thumb. Small. Automatic. Xiaoran’s heartbeat betrayed her anyway. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, Xiaoran tried again. And again. And very slowly, her tolerance actually improved. Not much, but enough that she could eat medium-spicy noodles without crying in public, which she considered a historic achievement.

“Wow,” Yuhao said one lunch break. “Love really changes people.”

“Exactly,” Xiaoran said proudly over her spicy hotpot.

Then her expression changed. Meilin narrowed her eyes.

“…Too spicy?”

Xiaoran’s eyes went watery.

“No.”

“Liar.”

“I’m fine.”

Then tears started rolling silently down her face. Yuhao lost it.

“She’s crying again.”

“I HATE ALL OF YOU.”

Yichen looked helpless as he pushed her drink closer.

“You pushed too hard again.”

“But I almost survived.”

“You’re literally sobbing.”

“That’s emotionally unrelated.”

Yichen laughed and handed her more tissues. Then, more softly—

“You know you don’t actually need to like spicy food because of me.”

Xiaoran sniffed.

“But you love it.”

“Hm.”

“And I wanted to experience things you like too.”

Oh. That one caught him off guard. Yichen looked at her for a second—flushed cheeks, watery eyes, all that stubborn sincerity she never bothered hiding. Then he smiled.

“You already do,” he said quietly.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

“You already understand my world enough.”

Silence.

Yuhao gagged. “Oh my god.”

Meilin nodded tiredly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran was too busy staring at Yichen to care, her heart melting embarrassingly fast. Then, after a pause—

“…I’m still learning spicy food.”

“Why?”

“So one day we can eat extra spicy hotpot together romantically.”

Yichen laughed and squeezed her hand under the table.

“Okay,” he said. “But we’re bringing milk.”

chapters.desc: A double date with the rival captain and the girl Xiaoran once fought on the café street. What could go wrong?
chapters.title: Should We Even Be Sitting Together?
chapters.epigraph: “Peace treaties are usually signed over food.”
chapters.content:
A double date with Zhou Yichen and Song Kai was already a terrible idea. Adding their girlfriends? Disaster. Especially because, technically, Lin Xiaoran and Xu Hani still hated each other after the Hair-Pulling Incident. Not publicly. Not dramatically. Just spiritually. Which was somehow worse. So when Song Kai suggested—

“Why don’t the four of us eat together once so things stop being awkward?”

—nobody was thrilled. Xu Hani looked offended. Xiaoran looked ready to commit crimes again. And Zhou Yichen immediately got a headache.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This is stupid,” Xiaoran hissed, fixing her hair outside the restaurant.

“It’s just dinner.”

“It’s diplomatic negotiations.”

Beside her, Yichen sighed. She wasn’t entirely wrong. Song Kai had picked a barbecue place by the river. Neutral territory, apparently. Very strategic. Yichen watched her mentally prepare for war.

“Remember,” he said calmly, “you promised not to fight.”

“I only fight when provoked.”

“That sentence inspires zero confidence.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“Why are YOU calm? Your rival is literally inside.”

“Basketball rival,” Yichen corrected.

“That’s still testosterone tension.”

Inside, Song Kai already looked exhausted.

“Hani,” he warned carefully, “please don’t provoke Xiaoran.”

“I don’t care about her enough to provoke her.”

Song Kai sighed. This dinner was going to kill him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, all four of them were sitting together. Painfully awkwardly. The restaurant was warm and noisy, meat sizzling on the grill in the middle of the table. Their table, though, was pure tension. Xu Hani drank water elegantly. Lin Xiaoran stabbed her grilled mushrooms like they’d wronged her. The two boys exchanged an exhausted look.

“Great atmosphere,” Song Kai muttered.

“No one’s bleeding yet,” Yichen answered.

“Amazing progress.”

Across the table, Hani suddenly spoke.

“So.” She looked at Xiaoran lazily. “Still fighting people over your boyfriend?”

Silence. Yichen closed his eyes. Here we go. Xiaoran smiled sweetly.

“Still talking too much?”

Song Kai grabbed his drink. Oh no. Yichen calmly put more meat in Xiaoran’s bowl before she could escalate. A distraction tactic. Very experienced boyfriend behavior. It only worked for a while.

“You know,” Hani continued casually, “Jun still laughs about that fight sometimes.”

“Good,” Xiaoran answered. “At least someone found meaning in your hair loss.”

Song Kai choked on his water. Yichen lowered his head, trying very hard not to laugh.

“Hani,” Song Kai warned tiredly.

“What?” Hani replied innocently.

“You too,” Yichen added quietly toward Xiaoran.

“I’m literally peaceful.”

“You threatened her hairstyle.”

“She started spiritually.”

“This sentence means nothing.”

It should have exploded already. Somehow it didn’t—mostly because the boys had gotten weirdly good at crisis management since dating these two. At one point, Hani complained about university applications and Xiaoran accidentally agreed with her. Both girls paused, like neither had expected common ground. The boys watched in silence, like scientists observing wild animals adapting to civilization. A waiter set a plate of extremely spicy meat in front of Hani instead of Xiaoran. Hani took a casual bite. Instant regret.

“…Why is this so spicy?!”

Xiaoran blinked—then burst out laughing. Not mocking. Genuinely helpless laughter.

“OH MY GOD.”

Hani glared with watery eyes.

“Why are you happy.”

“You look exactly like me last month.”

Yichen sighed. The spicy food incident. Traumatic memories. Song Kai looked more and more entertained as Xiaoran pushed a glass of milk toward Hani without thinking.

“Drink this before you pass away.”

“…Thanks.”

“You’re still annoying though.”

“Same to you.”

Progress. Questionable, but still progress.

Later, the conversation drifted back to basketball. Unfortunately. Song Kai smirked at Yichen.

“You still owe me a proper rematch.”

“You sound obsessed,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Because you got lucky.”

Xiaoran sat up straighter. Danger. Hani noticed too.

“Oh my god,” Hani muttered. “Look at her face.”

“What face?”

“The ‘don’t insult my boyfriend’ face.”

“I DON’T HAVE A FACE.”

“You absolutely do.”

Under the table, Yichen took Xiaoran’s wrist and gave it a gentle squeeze. Calm down. Song Kai laughed openly.

“She really gets angry over you instantly.”

“That’s because he’s talented,” Xiaoran said stubbornly.

Yichen looked tired.

“Xiaoran.”

“No. I’m serious.”

Hani looked at her strangely. Not mocking this time. Thoughtful.

“…You really like him huh?”

The whole table paused. The question sounded unexpectedly sincere, and even Xiaoran blinked, like the obviousness of the answer had surprised her for a second.

“Of course I do.”

No embarrassment, no joke. Just honest. The mood at the table shifted after that—softer, less hostile. Even Hani looked calmer, like she’d understood something. Beside her, Yichen had gone quiet. Hearing her answer like that, so naturally, still got to him every time. Then Song Kai ruined it.

“Disgusting,” he muttered.

Hani rolled her eyes.

“Your relationship is honestly exhausting to watch.”

“Thank you,” Xiaoran answered proudly.

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I accepted it anyway.”

Yichen finally laughed and put more meat on her plate, the way he always did without thinking. Watching that made Hani glance at Song Kai beside her. Song Kai looked suddenly horrified.

“…Don’t start.”

Too late. Across the table, Xiaoran noticed. A slow, dangerous smile spread across her face.

“Oh,” she whispered delightedly. “NOW who’s on a weird double date?”

chapters.desc: Fourteen days to find the perfect gift for a boy who already has everything—and remembers everything.
chapters.title: The Birthday Gift Problem
chapters.epigraph: “The best gifts aren’t bought. They’re remembered.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had exactly fourteen days before Zhou Yichen’s birthday. Which should’ve been enough time. Unfortunately, she was Lin Xiaoran, which meant a simple birthday present turned into a national crisis.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I don’t know what to buy him.”

Xiaoran lay face-down across Tang Meilin’s bed, suffering. Meilin kept doing her homework.

“You’ve been repeating that sentence for forty minutes.”

“Because LOVE is difficult.”

“Buying gifts isn’t love. It’s shopping.”

“Not for soulmates.”

Zhou Yichen was incredibly easy to please. Too easy. That was the problem. Basketball shoes? He’d smile. A hoodie? He’d smile. A handwritten note? He’d probably smile like an idiot. Which made choosing harder. Xiaoran wanted it to feel special. Not expensive. Just… important. Something that would make him think, Ah. This is so Xiaoran. Every idea felt stupid after five minutes.

“He already has shoes.”

“Then buy something else.”

“He has everything.”

“He doesn’t own a spaceship.”

“That’s because I’m poor.”

Meilin’s phone buzzed. She glanced at it.

“Oh.” Meilin looked up. “Yichen asked if you’re alive.”

Xiaoran groaned into the blankets.

“No one understands my suffering.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen, meanwhile, supposedly had no idea. Which was impressive, because Xiaoran was terrible at hiding things, especially excitement. Three days before his birthday, she followed him around school like a suspicious little criminal, disappeared at lunch, and came back looking stressed. Yuhao noticed.

“She’s planning something.”

“Obviously,” Yichen answered calmly.

“She looked at your wrist for thirty seconds earlier.”

Yichen paused. Interesting.

Later, at basketball practice, Yichen was sitting courtside with a water bottle when Xiaoran appeared out of nowhere. Too cheerful. Suspiciously cheerful.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Hypothetically.”

“Bad start already.”

“If someone gave you a birthday gift…” She sat down beside him casually. “What would mean the most to you?”

Yichen looked at her, then smiled a little.

“You’re asking for yourself?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Okay maybe.”

He laughed and wiped the sweat from his neck with a towel, which distracted Xiaoran for three full seconds. Ridiculously handsome athlete boyfriend. Very inconvenient. Then he answered honestly—

“Anything from you.”

“That’s NOT HELPFUL.”

“It’s true.”

“No, it’s vague.”

Yuhao, who had overheard everything, called over—

“Buy him matching underwear.”

“GET OUT.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem was that Zhou Yichen remembered everything. Her milk tea order. Her exam schedule. The exact bakery she liked. Random things she’d said months ago. Meanwhile, Xiaoran regularly lost her own phone. How was she supposed to compete with someone that thoughtful? Then one evening, sorting through old photos, Xiaoran froze. Inside a storage box was something she’d almost forgotten: the claw machine bunny. A little faded now. A tiny white rabbit. And she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first thing Zhou Yichen ever won for her, back before they were even dating. She had failed eleven times in a row; he’d stepped in and won it on the first try. Later, after they got together, she’d waved it at him and joked—

“If we ever break up in the future, I’m keeping this.”

And Yichen had said, completely calmly—

“We’re not breaking up.”

At the time, she’d laughed. Now, remembering it made her chest ache, because he had meant it, even back then. And suddenly Xiaoran knew exactly what to give him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen’s birthday arrived quietly. No big party. Just close friends having dinner at Yuhao’s house. Very normal. Very warm. Yuhao gave him basketball accessories. Meilin gave him practical stationery, because she valued function over romance. Then everyone looked at Xiaoran, who had suddenly become very nervous.

“Oh?” Yuhao grinned. “Special girlfriend gift.”

“Shut up.”

Yichen watched as she pulled out a medium-sized paper bag, her sleeves tugged down over her hands.

“…It’s not expensive,” she muttered.

“No one asked.”

“I’m managing expectations.”

Then she handed it to him. Yichen expected something cute. Maybe handmade. Maybe dramatic. Instead, he went still when he opened the box. Inside was the old white rabbit, carefully cleaned, with a simple silver bracelet around its neck. Small. Minimal. Exactly the kind he would actually wear every day. For a second, he said nothing, which made Xiaoran panic.

“Oh no.”

Yichen looked up.

“…You kept this?”

“Of course I kept it.”

Silence.

“You remembered?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…The claw machine?”

“No.” His voice went soft. “What you said afterward.”

Oh. That. Xiaoran’s face went hot. He remembered that too? The others looked lost.

“What are you two talking about?” Yuhao asked.

“History,” Meilin answered wisely.

Then Xiaoran looked at Yichen again.

“You said we wouldn’t break up.” She tried laughing lightly. “So I thought… maybe the rabbit should stay with the original owner for your birthday.”

The room was quiet for exactly two seconds. Then Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s sleeve.

“WHY ARE THEY LIKE THIS.”

“Quiet.”

Zhou Yichen was still looking at the bracelet, the rabbit, Xiaoran sitting there pretending not to panic. No expensive gift could have hit him harder. Lin Xiaoran always managed to give him things that felt frighteningly sincere. He reached over and took her hand.

“You know,” he murmured, “this might be my favorite gift ever.”

Xiaoran went red.

“Don’t say things like that publicly.”

“It’s my birthday.”

“That’s not how birthdays work.”

Yichen laughed, then put the bracelet on right there. Somehow that hit Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. It looked right on him, like it had always belonged there. Yuhao stared at them.

“I’m single because the universe hates me.”

Meilin nodded sympathetically.

“Correct.”

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has never cooked. Zhou Yichen’s parents are out on Saturday. She’s going to cook anyway.
chapters.title: This Tastes Suspiciously Edible
chapters.epigraph: “The secret ingredient is stubbornness.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran decided to cook for Zhou Yichen because of one dangerous thought: How hard could it be? Historically, that thought had ruined many lives.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve never cooked before.”

Tang Meilin said it in the tone of someone watching a preventable tragedy. They were in the supermarket, Xiaoran pushing the cart with terrifying confidence.

“I can learn.”

“You almost burned instant noodles last year.”

“That was a microwave issue.”

“You put METAL inside.”

“Technicality.”

Xiaoran kept tossing things into the cart: eggs, tomatoes, beef, green onions. Whatever she’d seen in cooking videos.

“…Do you even know what you’re making?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Silence.

“Love.”

“Okay we’re doomed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started innocently. Yesterday at lunch, Yichen had mentioned—

“My parents won’t be home Saturday.”

Xiaoran’s drama-poisoned brain immediately translated that into: perfect romantic cooking opportunity. Realistically, she should have ordered takeout and lied. But Lin Xiaoran had too much pride. If she was going to cook for her boyfriend, she was going to actually cook, even if civilization collapsed. So Friday night was preparation night: three hours of cooking tutorials, two breakdowns, and one nearly catastrophic knife incident.

“Your fingers are more important than romance,” Meilin warned over video call.

“I know.”

“Why are you holding the knife like that.”

“…Like a warrior?”

“Like a threat to society.”

Xiaoran kept chopping, badly. Cooking looked so much easier in videos. Why did onions require suffering? Why was the oil attacking her? Why did garlic burn in three seconds?!

“This is impossible.”

“It’s fried rice, not nuclear engineering.”

“You don’t understand pressure.”

Meilin understood perfectly. The pressure was Lin Xiaoran desperately wanting Zhou Yichen to like something she’d made herself. Which made the whole thing kind of cute. Dangerous. But cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and now Xiaoran was standing in Yichen’s kitchen in an apron, questioning every decision she had ever made. Yichen sat at the counter, watching. Too quietly.

“Why are you staring at me.”

“You invited me here.”

“To EAT. Not observe.”

“Hm.”

That calm little hm irritated her, mostly because he looked far too good sitting there in a grey hoodie, chin propped on one hand, watching her cook. Very distracting.

“You’re nervous,” he said after a while.

“I’m NOT nervous.”

“You added salt twice.”

Silence. Xiaoran looked down at the bowl. Oh no. OH NO. Yichen laughed under his breath while Xiaoran panicked.

“This is a disaster.”

“It’s fixable.”

“How.”

“We start over.”

No annoyance, no disappointment. Just calm. And somehow that made Xiaoran feel less stressed right away. Then Yichen got up and came over, close enough that Xiaoran forgot how to breathe normally. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

“You missed some eggshell too,” he murmured.

“…Where.”

Instead of answering, Yichen reached past her shoulder and carefully picked the tiny piece of shell out of the bowl. Warmth flooded Xiaoran’s face. Domestic Zhou Yichen should be illegal. Then he glanced down at her.

“…Cute apron.”

“Don’t mock me.”

“I’m serious.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Because it’s pink.”

“It was the only one Meilin had.”

Unfortunately, the pink apron had tiny strawberries on it, and Zhou Yichen was visibly fighting a laugh every five minutes. Unbearable man.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cooking actually improved after that, mostly because Yichen stopped sitting there and helped. Not taking over. Just helping—washing vegetables beside her, passing things, stopping her from committing seasoning crimes. At one point, Xiaoran frowned at the pan.

“Does this look cooked?”

Yichen leaned in to check. Way too close. Xiaoran could smell his shampoo again. Disaster.

“Hm,” he murmured thoughtfully. “Almost.”

Then he reached around her to turn the heat down—one arm beside her, his chest almost touching her shoulder—and Lin Xiaoran forgot about cooking entirely.

“…You’re distracting.”

“I’m fixing your fire hazard.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

Yichen smiled a little, then looked down at her in that quiet, soft way. The one that ruined her every time.

“What are you saying, then?” he asked softly.

Nothing. Her brain had stopped working again. Meanwhile, the rice was burning.

“OH MY GOD.”

Romance, interrupted. Tragic.

✦ ✦ ✦

An hour later, the food was done. And it looked… surprisingly normal. Actual edible-looking food. Xiaoran stared at the table.

“…Why does this look successful.”

Yichen sat across from her calmly.

“You worked hard.”

“That doesn’t guarantee quality.”

Then came the most terrifying moment of Xiaoran’s life: Yichen picking up the spoon. She watched him like a criminal awaiting sentencing.

“Be honest,” she warned. “If it’s bad, just say it.”

“Hm.”

“No boyfriend lies.”

“Hm.”

“And don’t force yourself.”

“I understand.”

Then he took a bite. Silence. One second. Two seconds. Three—

“…Wait.”

Xiaoran’s soul left her body.

“It’s bad?”

“No.”

He looked genuinely surprised. He looked at the food, then at her.

“…This is actually really good.”

“…What.”

“The beef’s seasoned properly.”

“The rice texture’s good too.”

Then Lin Xiaoran screamed.

“OH MY GOD.”

Yichen started laughing as Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“YOU’RE NOT LYING?”

“I’m not.”

“REALLY?”

“It’s genuinely good.”

Xiaoran dropped into her chair and covered her face.

“I’m talented.”

“You almost poisoned the kitchen earlier.”

“BUT NOT THE FOOD.”

The pride all over her face was adorable, and Yichen couldn’t stop smiling as she celebrated over fried rice like she’d won a national award.

“You know,” he said, taking another bite, “I thought this would taste terrible.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“I still came prepared to eat everything.”

“That’s NOT ROMANTIC.”

“It is from my perspective.”

Xiaoran glared at him. Yichen laughed again. After a moment, very casually, he reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear. Xiaoran forgot the entire conversation. Yichen looked at her flushed face and smiled.

“…You should cook for me again sometime.”

Somehow, that meant more to her than the food turning out well.

chapters.desc: A sudden downpour, a useless umbrella, and one sentence Lin Xiaoran really didn’t mean to say out loud.
chapters.title: Holding Hands Is Warm, But Hugging in the Rain Is Dangerous
chapters.epigraph: “Some storms are worth getting caught in.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated rain. Not emotionally. Physically. Rain ruined hair, shoes, makeup, moods, dignity, and occasionally public transport. Zhou Yichen, strangely, loved it. Not in a poetic way. He just liked the quiet, the cooler air, the way the basketball court smelled afterward. Today, though, the rain was dangerous for a completely different reason.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Run faster!”

“I AM RUNNING.”

“No you’re not, you’re tall-walking aggressively.”

They were sprinting through a sudden evening downpour after leaving the arcade downtown. Ten minutes ago, the weather had been perfect. Now? Total betrayal from the sky. Xiaoran held her bag over her head while Yichen tried to angle their one umbrella against a wind that seemed to have a personal grudge.

“This umbrella is decorative,” Xiaoran complained loudly.

“It’s trying its best.”

“WE’RE STILL DYING.”

Yichen laughed and pulled her closer by the wrist so she wouldn’t slip on the wet sidewalk. Even drenched, that small thing made her heart go soft. Very annoying. Finally they ducked under the awning of a closed bookstore, both breathing hard. Rain came down in silver sheets around them, headlights smeared across the wet street. And suddenly the whole thing felt unfairly romantic. Xiaoran noticed. Unfortunately. Rain still clung to Yichen’s hair. His sleeves were pushed halfway up, his shoulders soaked from shielding her. He looked disgustingly handsome, like one of those drama scenes that made audiences quit their jobs.

Zhou Yichen looked down at her.

“…Why are you staring.”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been quiet for thirty seconds.”

“That’s because rain lowers my IQ.”

“Hm.”

His thumb brushed across her knuckles absentmindedly. A small, automatic thing. But suddenly Xiaoran was hyperaware of everything: the sound of the rain, how close he was, how warm his hand was. Maybe because the weather felt softer, her chest did too.

“Holding hands is warm,” she mumbled.

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

Oops. Accidental thought leak. Xiaoran looked away.

“Nothing.”

But Zhou Yichen always got curious at the worst possible times.

“What did you say?”

Silence. Then, defiantly—

“I said holding hands is warm.”

“And?”

She hesitated. Why did this suddenly feel embarrassing? Then, softly—

“…But hugging feels warmer.”

Silence. When Xiaoran finally looked up, Yichen was watching her quietly. Not teasing. Not laughing. Just looking at her with that soft expression that always made her weak. Then, slowly, he let go of her hand. Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

Instead of answering, Yichen stepped closer and, without a word, pulled her into his arms. Warmth wrapped around her. Not sudden. Just steady. His hoodie smelled faintly like rain and laundry detergent, and one hand settled at the back of her head. Xiaoran understood something then. Holding hands was warm. But this was dangerous. Hugging Zhou Yichen in the cold rain made the whole world quietly disappear—the noisy street, the weather, the passing cars—until there was only the steady beat of his heart under her cheek.

Above her head, Yichen murmured—

“Better?”

His voice was lower like this. Closer. Xiaoran tightened her arms around him.

“…A little.”

“A little?”

“Okay maybe a lot.”

He laughed under his breath, and she felt it against her forehead. This relationship was medically unsafe. Outside their little shelter, the rain kept pouring. Neither of them moved. Xiaoran had become emotionally attached to this hug, and Yichen apparently had no intention of letting go either. After a while, very quietly—

“You’re cold,” he murmured.

“That’s because SOMEONE gave me fake umbrella protection.”

“Hm.”

“That hm means guilt.”

“No it doesn’t.”

“It absolutely does.”

Yichen smiled and rubbed her arm through her damp cardigan, trying to warm her up. That small thing got to her more than any grand gesture could. Then thunder cracked overhead. Xiaoran flinched, and Yichen’s arms tightened around her before he even thought about it. The realization hit her embarrassingly hard. Being loved by Zhou Yichen was genuinely unfair sometimes. Then, quietly—

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I think rain might actually be romantic.”

“Only now?”

“I’m growing as a person.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“It is.”

He laughed softly again. After a moment, Yichen looked down at her. Close. Way too close. The rain blurred behind him and the yellow streetlights caught in his eyes, and Xiaoran’s heartbeat went ridiculous again. This was exactly like the drama scenes she screamed over. Except better, because it was real.

“You have a habit,” Yichen murmured.

“What.”

“You say dangerous things casually.”

“I do not.”

“Hugging is warmer?”

Silence. Okay. Maybe she did. Xiaoran buried her face deeper in his chest.

“I take it back.”

“Too late.”

“Delete the memory.”

“Impossible.”

After a second, he kissed the top of her damp hair. Soft and quick. And that tiny kiss destroyed whatever dignity she had left.

“This relationship,” she whispered weakly, “is making me too happy.”

chapters.desc: A teacher’s wedding, one cream-colored dress, and the evening Zhou Yichen forgot how to talk.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Looks Beautiful Today
chapters.epigraph: “He had seen her every day. He had never seen her like this.”
chapters.content:
At exactly 5:42 p.m., Zhou Yichen realized Lin Xiaoran looked too beautiful today. Not everyday cute. Dangerous. The kind that made him briefly forget how conversations worked. Which irritated him a little, because he prided himself on composure. That composure disappeared the second Xiaoran stepped out of Tang Meilin’s room.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You can breathe now.”

Yuhao’s voice snapped him back to reality. He looked deeply entertained, because Zhou Yichen had frozen. For three full seconds. They were waiting downstairs at Meilin’s apartment before heading to Teacher Su’s wedding banquet. Teacher Su taught literature and had somehow become everyone’s emotional support teacher, so a few of her closest students had been invited—including some unfairly attractive teenagers. Specifically, Lin Xiaoran. She came down the stairs slowly, fiddling with one small earring, and Yichen’s brain stopped working again.

Xiaoran almost never dressed up. Usually it was oversized sweaters, school uniform, hoodies—his, often. Tonight she wore a soft cream dress that fell just below her knees. Simple. Elegant. Not trying to look older. Just pretty. Her hair was curled at the ends, framing her face. Tiny pearl earrings. Light makeup. She still looked completely like herself, just prettier, in a way that felt unfair to society. Xiaoran looked nervous the second she noticed everyone staring.

“…Why are you all acting weird.”

Meilin crossed her arms proudly.

“Because I worked hard.”

“Meilin spent forty minutes fixing your hair,” Yuhao informed.

“I almost lost my life,” Meilin corrected.

Then she looked at Yichen, and paused. Her boyfriend was staring. Not subtly. Not composed. Completely focused on her.

“…Why are YOU acting weird?”

Yichen blinked. Twice. Still staring. Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing beside him.

“Oh my god.”

Then, quietly, Yichen said—

“You look beautiful.”

Zhou Yichen almost never gave compliments that directly. His were usually smaller, softer, private. This one came out on instinct, before he could think, and it hit Xiaoran harder than any dramatic flirting could. Her whole face went red.

“…Oh.”

Brilliant response. Yichen seemed a little calmer now that he’d said it. His eyes kept moving over her face anyway, still taking her in, and Xiaoran noticed, which only made it worse.

“Stop looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like…” She gestured helplessly. “Like THIS.”

Yuhao cut in—

“He looks like he just discovered women.”

“Shut up.”

Meilin sighed into her soul.

“Can we leave before these two combust.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The banquet was warm and lively: golden lights, soft music, round tables full of chatting relatives and teachers. The students sat together off to one side, trying to behave. Keyword: trying. Teacher Su looked so happy that it made everyone emotional, especially when she nearly cried at the sight of her former students all dressed up.

“You all grew up so fast,” she sniffed.

Xiaoran hugged her carefully, then ruined the moment immediately—

“Teacher, you look like a movie star today.”

Teacher Su laughed through tears.

“Still talking nonsense.”

Yichen stood nearby holding the gift bag. And once again, he looked at Xiaoran and lost his train of thought. It kept happening all evening—the way she smiled politely at older relatives, the way she laughed, the way the warm light caught her earrings.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He blinked. Teacher Su smiled knowingly.

“You’ve been staring at Xiaoran all evening.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her tea. The other students choked trying not to laugh. Even Meilin looked spiritually revived. Outwardly, Yichen stayed calm. Inwardly, not at all. The tips of his ears gave him away. Teacher Su continued smiling warmly.

“You two are very cute together.”

Xiaoran buried her face in her hands.

“This wedding is attacking me personally.”

Yichen looked away, the corner of his mouth lifting, which only made everything worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, as the guests began to leave, a light rain started outside the hotel entrance—soft enough not to matter. The others waited for their rides while Xiaoran and Yichen stood a little apart under the decorative lights by the garden path. A quiet moment. Warm night air. Everything felt softer. Xiaoran looked down at her shoes.

“…Do I really look beautiful?”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What kind of question is that.”

“You kept staring.”

Silence.

“Because you do.”

Xiaoran looked away fast. Why did simple compliments from him feel so dangerous? Yichen stepped closer, close enough that his suit jacket brushed her sleeve. He looked unfair tonight too. Black formalwear should be banned for teenage boys. Especially Zhou Yichen.

“I think everyone noticed,” Xiaoran mumbled.

“What?”

“That you kept looking at me.”

“Hm.”

“Hm means yes.”

“It’s hard not to.”

Silence. Was he trying to kill her tonight? Yichen looked thoughtful, like he wanted to say something else. Then, very quietly—

“You know what scared me earlier?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“What?”

“When you came downstairs.”

“…Why?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Because for one second,” he admitted softly, “I genuinely forgot how to talk.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

chapters.desc: One secondhand poetry book. One very dramatic girlfriend. One week nobody at school will ever forget.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Became a Poetry Menace
chapters.epigraph: “Even ordinary afternoons become literature.”
chapters.content:
It started because Lin Xiaoran bought one old poetry book at a secondhand bookstore. One book. That was all it took to destroy the peace.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It smells intellectual.”

Tang Meilin stared at the dusty hardcover in horror. The four of them were at a café on Saturday while Xiaoran proudly showed off her purchase: an old, faded hardcover of translated classical poetry and romantic prose. She already looked like a changed woman.

“It’s vintage,” she corrected seriously.

“It smells like someone’s grandfather.”

“That’s called history.”

Yichen glanced at it, stirring his iced coffee.

“Do you even like poetry?”

“I’m evolving.”

Yuhao looked suspicious.

“Last month you said philosophy was fake.”

“That was before literature entered my soul.”

Meilin sighed.

“We’re doomed.”

Unfortunately, she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday morning, Lin Xiaoran was unbearable. Not normal unbearable. Poetic unbearable, which was worse. She leaned against her desk in the morning sun and sighed—

“Some people,” she sighed, “are like moonlight reflected across water.”

Silence. Meilin looked up from her homework.

“…What.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Beautiful but impossible to hold.”

Yuhao stared. Zhou Yichen stopped writing and slowly looked at her. Where was this coming from? Then, calmly—

“Good morning to you too.”

Xiaoran nodded wisely.

“The moon also rises gently.”

“I hate this already,” Meilin muttered.

It got worse. Much worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch, Yuhao stole a dumpling off Xiaoran’s plate. Instead of yelling like a normal person, she narrowed her eyes and whispered:

“Greed is a fire that consumes friendship.”

Yuhao froze.

“…What.”

“Ancient wisdom.”

“You literally threatened me spiritually.”

“That dumpling had meaning.”

Yichen nearly smiled into his drink. Watching Xiaoran weaponize poetry all day was getting more entertaining by the hour, especially because she so clearly felt intelligent now. Then she turned to him. Danger.

“What.”

Xiaoran pointed her chopsticks at him.

“You know,” she murmured, “there’s a phrase here that reminds me of you.”

Silence. Yichen leaned back.

“Hm?”

“‘The pine tree does not bend easily before winter winds.’”

Meilin gagged. Yuhao looked horrified. Xiaoran went on proudly—

“It means someone calm and steadfast.”

“I know what pine trees symbolize,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Oh.”

“But thank you.”

He said it simply, gently, and it got to Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. Zhou Yichen always took her nonsense seriously. Even poetic nonsense.

“You’re not making fun of me?”

“Should I?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

Meilin watched the interaction with dead eyes.

“I’m dropping out of school.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem started on Wednesday, because Xiaoran had memorized too many lines. Way too many. Now she ambushed people with them all day. At PE class—

“The wind today feels lonely.”

During math—

“Numbers are humanity’s attempt to organize chaos.”

While eating crackers—

“Crisp sounds remind us life is fragile.”

Yuhao finally snapped.

“WHO GAVE HER THIS BOOK.”

In afternoon study hall, Yichen sat beside Xiaoran while she copied poetry into a notebook—concentrating hard, a tiny frown on her face, completely serious. Dangerously cute. Then, without looking up—

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“If I died young, would you compare me to flowers?”

Silence. Yichen slowly turned toward her.

“…What kind of sentence is that.”

“It’s literary.”

“It’s concerning.”

Xiaoran finally looked up.

“In poetry, beautiful people always die tragically.”

“You’re not dying.”

“That sounds possessive.”

“It IS possessive.”

Xiaoran smiled—small and soft, like that answer pleased her far too much. Yichen noticed, and that tiny expression got to him too.
